title: Kabir the weaver
hook: Kabir of Benares, a weaver, sang in plain speech that no priest or custom stood between the soul and God

segments.voice: Yesterday, bhagat: truth has many singers. Today, the first of two Bhagats this path stays with for a while.

Benares, on the Ganges: temples, priests, pilgrims, scholars arguing in Sanskrit. And in a narrow lane, the clack of a handloom. A weaver sits at it, throwing the shuttle back and forth, singing as he works. Not in Sanskrit. In the plain speech of the street, sharp enough to make a priest wince and a laborer laugh. His name was Kabir, and the Sikh Gurus kept his songs in their book.
screen: `BENARES, THE HOLY CITY.` → `A LOOM IN A LANE.` → `A WEAVER, SINGING.`

segments.voice: Honest start: very little about Kabir's life is certain, and scholars disagree about his dates. In his own verses he calls himself a julaha, a weaver; tradition says he grew up in a Muslim weaving family in Benares and learned from the Hindu teacher Ramanand. Beyond that, much of what's told is legend. His songs are what remain, and the Guru Granth Sahib keeps a great many of them. What did he sing? That nothing stands between the soul and God: not the priest, not the mullah, not birth, not pilgrimage. In a hymn in Rag Gauri he turns on caste pride with a joke: if you're a Brahmin, born of a Brahmin mother, why didn't you come into the world by some other way? Everyone arrives the same way. He was just as blunt about empty ritual in any religion. And the loom? In a hymn in Rag Gujri, his mother weeps: how will these children live? Kabir has given up spinning and weaving and written God's Name on his body. Kabir answers that while threading the shuttle he forgets his Beloved, and that one Provider looks after them all. So he made no neat peace with his trade. But he never stopped thinking like a weaver. In Rag Asa he calls God the weaver whose secret no one knows, who stretched the warp of the whole world, earth and sky for a loom, sun and moon for two shuttles. A weaver's own tools became his picture of God at work. Hence today's line: the loom is the prayer.
screen: `KABIR — A WEAVER OF BENARES.` · `LITTLE KNOWN, MUCH SUNG.` · `NO ONE STANDS BETWEEN.` · `GOD THE WEAVER, EARTH AND SKY THE LOOM.` · then, large: `THE LOOM IS THE PRAYER.`

segments.voice: Choose one task in front of you today: a job, a class, the dishes, a child's bedtime. Picture doing it the way Kabir sat at the loom, attentive, steady, every motion counted, not rushing to be done. If you pray, let the rhythm of the work carry a word you remember by; if not, let it carry the breath.
Julaha, weaver. Kabir, a weaver of Benares whose plain, sharp songs, kept in the Guru Granth Sahib, say nothing stands between the soul and God.
Your line: the loom is the prayer. Even a shuttle can point to God. Day two hundred fifty-three, done.

howItsDone: Kabir's hymns in the Guru Granth Sahib are sung in Sikh kirtan alongside the Gurus' own, in the same ragas.

fork.setup: a proud Brahmin tells Kabir that birth makes him holier. what does Kabir's hymn answer?
options: he jokes: if you're so different, why didn't you come into the world some other way?
fork.reveal: in Rag Gauri, Kabir points out that everyone is born the same way; caste pride has nothing to stand on.

original.note: Gurmukhi: Kabir; an Arabic word, al-Kabir, 'the Great', one of the names of God in Islam.

trapdoor: what you thought: Kabir was a holy man who left the world.
what it means: a working weaver whose songs say nothing stands between the soul and God, and who pictured God as a weaver at the loom of the world.
what a scholar hears: a julaha, as he calls himself, whose dates and biography are uncertain; in Asa he names God koree, the weaver, with earth and sky for a loom.

sources.ref: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 324 (Gauri Kabir: 'if you are a Brahmin, born of a Brahmin mother')
Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 524 (Gujri Kabir: Kabir's mother weeps over the loom; Kabir answers)
Guru Granth Sahib, Asa Kabir, around Ang 484 (koree ko kaahoo maram na jaanaa: God the weaver, earth and sky the loom, sun and moon the shuttles)

notes: Editor review (2026-10-01): SERIOUS fix: the teach said Kabir 'never left the loom' and that the loom and the Name were one job, but the cited Gujri hymn (Ang 524) says the opposite: he has given up weaving, his mother weeps 'how will these children live' (not 'this boy'), and Kabir says threading the shuttle makes him forget his Beloved. The loom-as-prayer line now rests on Asa Kabir (God as the weaver, earth and sky the loom). Also removed uncited dates ('six hundred years', 'fifteenth century'), superlatives ('holiest city', 'most hymns of all') and the manuscript claim in the trapdoor.
Word is the title's head per the outline.
Kabir's dates (fifteenth century; traditional dates 1398–1518 are disputed) and his Muslim julaha family are stated cautiously; Ramanand as teacher is marked as tradition.
The Brahmin hymn (jau tu brahman brahmanee jaaiaa, tau aan baat kaahe nahee aaiaa) cited to Gauri Kabir, Ang 324; confirm Ang.
The mother's lament (muse muse rovai kabir kee maaee) cited to Gujri Kabir, Ang 524; confirm Ang and paraphrase.
The Guru Granth Sahib as among the oldest written sources for Kabir's verses is a common scholarly claim; confirm wording.
Restyled 2026-10-07 (job 2): voice tightened; content and sources unchanged.
